title: Security threats depend on attacker access
lead: Locate the attacker’s control before naming the ML attack mechanism.
bullets: Poisoning: altered learning inputs influence the trained model.
Inference manipulation: altered production inputs affect an existing model’s output.
Privacy inference: access can reveal sensitive membership or attributes.
Assumptions matter: access, knowledge, and goals differ by threat.
example: A compromised CRM writer could affect current inputs; those records create a poisoning path only if later used for training.
takeaway: The accidental CRM migration remains a different scenario.

title: Enforce access at the resource boundary
lead: Authentication, authorization, validation, and audit solve different parts of the problem.
bullets: Authenticate: establish caller identity.
Authorize: check operation, resource, and scope.
Validate: enforce the input contract independently.
Audit: preserve useful access and change evidence.
example: The scorer may read the approved M1 artifact; it must not gain permission to promote M2 merely by reaching the registry.
takeaway: A trust boundary needs an enforced policy, not only a box on a diagram.

title: Least privilege follows responsibilities
lead: Separate source writes, candidate creation, release approval, and campaign use.
bullets: Scope identities to the operations and resources they need.
Separate duties: training does not imply release authority.
Protect credentials and avoid secrets in code or broad logs.
Review changes: connect access, source updates, and approvals.
example: A campaign user reads an approved score view, not unrestricted training data or production deployment credentials.
takeaway: This abbreviated teaching matrix is a starting point, not a complete bank permission design.

title: Privacy: expose what each role needs
lead: Campaign use and incident investigation require different views of customer information.
bullets: Minimize collection and the information exposed in outputs.
Separate views: campaigns and investigators have different purposes.
Protect logs and define retention and access rules.
Preserve accountability without making raw evidence broadly available.
example: Campaign staff may need Ana’s approved score and eligibility context; investigators may need restricted versioned evidence.
takeaway: Privacy is an access-and-data-use design, not a label attached to a technique.

title: Privacy techniques have specific limits
lead: Choose a mechanism for a defined objective rather than claiming privacy by technique name.
bullets: Specify the objective: what information should be protected from whom?
Tokens and synthetic data do not automatically establish anonymity.
Federation changes data location, not every leakage risk.
DP needs a defined protected unit and accounting across releases; no derivation here.
example: Protecting one transaction differs from protecting all contributions of a bank customer.
takeaway: Do not announce a guarantee without its assumptions and evidence.
